en: The *Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*, Chapter on the Cultivation of Loving-kindness, in one fascicle.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Divākara of Khotan and others under Imperial Commission during the Tang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with [an assembly of]...
A great assembly of bodhisattvas was gathered together, with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya as their leader.

At that time, ten billion Brahmā deities from the eastern quarter, all abiding in a mind of loving-kindness, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and made offerings to the Buddha with various exquisite gifts.
Having completed their offerings, they each sat upon lotus seats produced from a multitude of merits; with reverence and respect, they gazed up at the Tathāgata.
The Brahmās who had come from the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir all did likewise.
At that time, the assembly of Brahmā deities were in the presence of the Buddha;
each gazed upon the others with eyes of loving-kindness, and then, at the same moment, they all relaxed their countenances and looked intently at Maitreya Bodhisattva.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Virtuous World-Honored One!

The Omniscient One has attained perfect awakening to the nature of all phenomena and universally knows the wholesome and unwholesome karma of sentient beings, by which the ignorant wander through birth and death.
He is skillfully able to awaken them to the paths of the three vehicles, as well as how these three vehicles ultimately converge in the Single Vehicle.

Regarding the differences in the faculties and natures of all beings, and the presence of the Tathāgata-garbha within the entanglements and obscurations of their afflictions, he perceives them all clearly and without error.
Furthermore, he knows that all phenomena are entirely empty—like dreams, illusions, and mirages—and lack any solid reality;

yet his great compassion is inexhaustible. Through skillful means, he causes ordinary beings to perceive the subtle and wondrous marks of the Buddha’s form-body (*rūpakāya*). This Buddha-body is accomplished through the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); it is spontaneously real, eternally abiding and unchanging, just like space. If there are sentient beings who diligently cultivate merit and wisdom, who do not follow the fluctuations of their mental consciousnesses by racing toward external objects—unlike thirsty deer in the wilderness who pursue a mirage, taking it for water—such people will then behold the Buddha, constantly hear him preach the Dharma, and be able to practice according to the teachings in accordance with reason.
"Bhagavān!
I now wish to ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha a few questions; I only pray that you will, out of compassion, explain them for me."
World-Honored One!
How can a bodhisattva, with little exertion of effort, in peace and happiness without weariness, swiftly realize the vast Buddha-dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
“How does a bodhisattva dwell within birth and death without being oppressed by immeasurable sufferings, and swiftly bring all Buddha-dharmas to full completion?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying:
“Excellent, Maitreya!”
"You have always questioned me on various matters;
the meaning of what you ask now is most in accord with my own mind.

Out of compassion for all the devas and humans, and for all beings in the world, you are able to ask me such a question for the sake of great benefit and great peace for immeasurable sentient beings."
"I shall now analyze and expound this for you, so that all bodhisattvas may, without undergoing toil or hardship, swiftly realize the Buddha-enlightenment.
O Son of the Buddha!"

If there are sentient beings who, seeking bodhi, cultivate various practices and vows to always abide in peace and happiness, they should cultivate a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) to discipline themselves.

By practicing in this way, in every thought-moment they will constantly and fully practice the six *pāramitās*, swiftly reaching the stages of patience (*kṣānti*), and quickly attaining the perfection of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. They will be endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, the thirty-two marks, and the eighty minor characteristics, their bodies adorned with the most supreme merits;
and until the end of the future, they will forever dwell in peace and happiness.
It can also eliminate all the heavy karmic obstructions of sentient beings that have existed since beginningless time.
"O Son of the Buddha!

If Bodhisattvas cultivate a mind of loving-kindness, they should dwell in a secluded and tranquil place, gathering all mental factors through pure faith, and observe that the various limbs and joints of their bodies are all merely aggregates of atoms, formed by the combination of earth, water, fire, and wind."
Furthermore, one should contemplate that within each and every atom there is empty space;
that all such spaces have as their characteristic the capacity for containment.
Moreover, one should visualize those atoms as pure and translucent—outwardly like lapis lazuli and inwardly like purple-gold—exquisitely adorned, supple, and fragrant.

Furthermore, one should observe all sentient beings in all worlds; for every single sentient being, for every one of their limbs and joints, and for every atom within each limb and joint, it is exactly the same.

When Bodhisattvas have formed such a definitive understanding regarding their own bodies, the bodies of others, and all sentient beings, they should further contemplate their own body as being composed of atoms, wherein each and every atom contains a Buddha-land.

Within these lands, the palaces are made of lapis lazuli, with gates of white silver and pillars of gold; they are vast, lofty, and magnificent, with light and shadows penetrating through them. Precious halls stand in rows, surrounded by precious walls, and jeweled pavilions and towers are distributed everywhere.
Within each of these are celestial jewel-beds, upon which layered carpets and exquisite cushions are spread.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable, supreme, and excellent gardens surrounding and adorning it;

within these gardens were bathing pools, all with embankments made of the seven treasures, surrounded on all four sides by golden railings. Pure springs flowed continuously into them, with fragrant powders forming the mud and golden sand interspersed throughout.
The water of eight virtues filled them, clear and pure, while *pāṭala*, *utpala*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers bloomed and spread across their surfaces.
The four sides of that pond are lined with many precious trees, their flowers made of pearls, radiant and flourishing;
their fruits are fully matured, endowed with perfect fragrance and flavor.
Beneath each tree is placed a celestial jeweled throne, and before every throne, rows of precious vessels stand filled to the brim with ambrosial delicacies.
Furthermore, one should form this mental visualization: all these Buddha-lands have ground made of deep blue lapis lazuli, adorned with an intermingling array of various wonderful seven-jewels.

Within these lands, all the atoms are pure, subtle, and exquisite, like celestial jewels; their radiance is brilliant like the blazing midday sun; their color is beautiful like Jāmbūnada gold; their fragrance is pervasive like uraga-sandalwood; and their substance is soft and supple like kāñcana-cloth, capable of producing joy and pleasure when touched by the body.
"Having performed this contemplation, one should then form this thought: 'May all sentient beings from every world in the eastern direction come to enter the palaces within my Buddha-land;
likewise for all sentient beings in the worlds of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.'"

Furthermore, one should form this mental visualization: all sentient beings of these six realms possess identical deportment and similar physical characteristics; their bodies are supple and constantly fragrant; they possess the marks of a great man, fully adorned and majestic; they are free from all suffering and affliction, and experience celestial bliss.

If these sentient beings require clothing or articles of adornment, they immediately go beneath the kalpavṛkṣa trees; whatever they require is obtained according to their thoughts, with various implements serving as beautiful ornaments.

It is like the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin), where fragrant winds blow from the eight directions; when these winds touch their bodies, they cause their minds to be joyful and contented. There are musical instruments that no one strikes, yet they move back and forth with the wind, producing wondrous sounds.

These sentient beings may dwell in palaces, or roam through gardens and groves; some partake of the exquisite foods of the devas, while others hold precious vessels to drink the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*). Some sit upon lotus pedestals, adorned with necklaces that drape down on both sides; their wealth and treasures are abundant, and all necessities are fully provided. They enjoy various pleasures according to their inclinations, their countenances radiant and joyful, their bodies and minds delighted. Their bodies are forever free from illness; they possess the vigor of youth and beauty, neither aging nor dying. Their merit and power are all of one kind;
none are subject to the commands of others, and they are all able to utterly destroy lust, anger, and ignorance, destined to realize *bodhi* and attain ultimate peace and happiness.
"O Son of the Buddha!

When one who cultivates loving-kindness is among such sentient beings, if they see a single being who opposes them and their mind, focusing upon this person, fails to give rise to affection, they should deeply observe themselves with wisdom:
'In past lives, I must have committed grave karmic obstructions against this person; for this reason, that person now obstructs my bodhi today.'"
If I do not give rise to joy toward this person, then I likewise ought not to bring benefit to all other sentient beings. Why is this?
Since beginningless time, within the cycle of birth and death, there is not a single sentient being who has not once harmed me in the past;
if I do not give rise to compassion for these beings, I shall likewise do so toward all others.
I now universally bring benefit to all sentient beings; therefore, I must certainly maintain loving-kindness toward them.

Furthermore, one should reflect that the causes and conditions of anger can cause sentient beings to fall into hell, and if one harbors resentment, one will surely be reborn among venomous snakes in a future life.
If I were to receive such retribution in a future existence, I would instead cause that person’s intentions to be deeply satisfied.
Therefore, one should abandon all hearts of anger, resentment, and enmity.
If I were full of anger and enmity, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, currently residing in the ten directions, would all see me and think:
"How is it that this person, who seeks to attain bodhi, gives rise to anger and enmity?"
"Because these deluded people are possessed by hatred and resentment, they cannot liberate themselves from their own sufferings; how then could they possibly save all sentient beings?
Sentient beings with much anger will have bodies filled with evil poison throughout every life they take.

Therefore, one should cultivate a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, forever distancing oneself from hatred and the knots of enmity, and with perfect equanimity, bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings."
"If one contemplates in this manner and has thus become free from the fetter of hatred,
one should next visualize that the Buddhas of the ten directions, together with the bodhisattvas and the great assembly of śrāvakas, all come together and enter the palaces within my buddha-field."

The bodies of these Tathāgatas were one and a half times the height of ordinary humans; they were endowed with all the primary and secondary marks, upright and pure, their bodies adorned with celestial garments. Each sat upon a lion throne of a thousand-petaled lotus, surrounded by immeasurable multitudes. Precious canopies covered them above, and various jeweled banners were suspended. Necklaces and garlands hung down on all sides. Celestial musical instruments played spontaneously without being struck, their sounds harmonious and elegant, bringing joy to those who heard them. A fragrant breeze moved gently, blowing through the jeweled trees so that the banners, canopies, nets, and necklaces produced wondrous sounds, singing praises of the various merits of the Tathāgatas.

The vessels were made of gold and adorned with the seven treasures; their radiance was like that of the sun and moon, and their fragrance was like that of solid black sandalwood. Filled with ambrosia, they were used to make offerings to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the assembly of Śrāvakas. All those Bodhisattvas and Arhats, moreover, sported in joy within the supreme Dharma of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, one should visualize that all sentient beings are seated before the thrones of all Buddhas, and that the Buddhas expound for them the practice of cultivating loving-kindness (*maitrī*), just as I am now practicing it; their speech is exquisite and harmonious, gladdening their hearts and causing all sentient beings to attain the most supreme bliss.
It is like a person who obtains ambrosial nectar and uses it to bathe and wash away their weariness and toil, so that both body and spirit are refreshed and at ease;
this is also like that: by moistening the mind with the Dharma, one extinguishes all afflictions, attaining tranquility of body and mind and obtaining eternal peace and happiness.

Furthermore, one should form this mental visualization: all these precious banners, pennants, canopies, robes, and other such objects consist of atoms that emit a brilliant radiance surpassing the sun; they are soft, supple, and smooth to the touch like a celestial body; the fragrance they emit is like that of gośīrṣa-candana; their color is pure like vaidūrya gem; and the images of all things appear within them.

Furthermore, one should form this mental visualization: within each and every Tathāgata, the atoms of their bodies become increasingly soft, radiant, and exquisite in color, surpassing the previous atoms by more than a hundred thousandfold.

Furthermore, one should observe that all sentient beings whom I have in mind are empty of intrinsic nature and devoid of self, being like a dream, like an illusion, like a mirage, and like a visual impairment;
all Buddhas are likewise so, for their own nature is entirely empty and fundamentally without a self.
Ordinary beings lack wisdom; they falsely cling to the notion that there is a self-nature within those [phenomena], and for this reason, they are unable to be liberated from birth and death.

Furthermore, one should observe that the essence and characteristics of all dharmas are subtle, entirely empty and quiescent. Yet ordinary beings give rise to various objective realms through their own conceptual discrimination; within these very discriminations, they bind themselves. Until they have realized the self-nature of the mind, for as long as that time lasts, they remain as if in a dream, falsely attached to various objects.
Furthermore, one should observe that all three realms are entirely empty; emptiness does not obstruct emptiness, yet my present mind of loving-kindness remains narrow and small.

Moreover, one should reflect: "Just as all sentient beings and all Buddhas are by nature empty and without self, I should know that my own body is likewise so, and all lands are nothing but mental conceptions."

“Having formed this understanding, one should further observe that within every single atom of all those atoms, there are the Buddha-lands of the three periods of time. These lands are supremely pure, surpassing all previously mentioned Buddha-lands, and are fully endowed with the Buddhas of the three periods, the sentient beings of the three periods, and all manner of adornments throughout the three periods.”

The kalpas of the three periods of time enter into a single thought-moment; within each and every thought-moment, the Buddhas of the three periods of time sit in all places, universally appearing before all sentient beings—sometimes entering meditative concentration, sometimes preaching the wondrous Dharma, sometimes partaking of fine food, or sometimes drinking sweet dew. Before each Buddha, Bodhisattvas and Arhats of the three periods of time sit in surrounding circles, their bodies filled with the bliss of the three periods of time.
One also sees one’s own body in the presence of these Buddhas, receiving such peace and happiness throughout the three periods of time.

Furthermore, one should form this mental visualization: within each and every thought-moment, my bodies throughout the three periods of time each hold immeasurable, supreme offerings to make offerings to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas, as well as to bestow them upon the various classes of sentient beings.

In every single thought-moment, various clouds of fragrance issue forth from his body; within these clouds are immeasurable jeweled canopies, exquisitely adorned and decorated, which completely cover all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and all sentient beings of the six realms.

Those clouds further rained down the nectar of heaven, as well as fine black gośīrṣa sandalwood powder, *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, *pundarīka* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, *puṇḍarīka* flowers, *sugandha* flowers, and *sumana* flowers; all fell in profusion from the sky.
The lightning flashed with fierce brilliance like the sun spreading its radiance, and the sound of thunder shook the earth, bringing joy to all who heard it.

All Buddhas, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and sentient beings—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—experienced the most supreme peace and bliss within their four modes of conduct at all times.
“O Son of the Buddha!

It is like a bhikṣu who enters the meditative concentration of the universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*), perceiving all things as earth, or as water, fire, and wind, and thereby maintaining his mind through such perceptions;
so too is it for one who cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*), adorning and maintaining the mind through the sublime resolve of loving-kindness.”
Furthermore, one should reflect: "The peace and happiness I now bestow upon sentient beings are merely conceptual constructs, like illusions and transformations;
just as a magician performs illusory feats, so too do I provide various forms of peace and happiness to all sentient beings."
Furthermore, just as illusory objects have no intrinsic nature, so it is with all sentient beings: from the very beginning, they lack the nature of a self or what belongs to a self.
Again, just as a thirsty deer, amidst a mirage, falsely conceives the notion of water and exhausts itself in pursuit of it, one should know that my practice of loving-kindness is likewise so.
Furthermore, just as water cannot be found in a mirage, so it is with all phenomena: they likewise lack a self-nature.

Again, just as one sees various objects in a dream and the dreaming mind discriminates them, taking them to be real things, yet upon waking finds they have no location at all—one should know that all phenomena are exactly like this.

It is like a person with cataracts who, within the clear sky, perceives various objects and claims they exist; later, when that person obtains *agada* medicine and the cataracts are completely cured, all the perceived objects vanish accordingly.

In the same way, because sentient beings possess the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), they harbor the notion of a self (*ātman*). If they obtain the medicine of wisdom and eliminate these views, the notion of a self likewise ceases.
Therefore, I should cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*) in this way: like awakening from a dream, free from the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self.

Son of the Buddha, you should know that one who cultivates this loving-kindness—even if they have not yet abandoned conceptual discrimination and have not yet ceased the views of "self" and "what belongs to self"—will constantly obtain the merit of the six Brahma-abodes.

If, however, they relinquish discrimination and depart from the views of "self" and "what belongs to self," this is called "vast loving-kindness. All karmic obstructions accumulated since previous lifetimes will be completely extinguished, and before long, they shall realize unsurpassed bodhi.
“O Son of the Buddha!
All bodhisattvas should cultivate a mind of loving-kindness in this manner; because you have cultivated loving-kindness, you are called a ‘loving one.
O Son of the Buddha!”

If any son or daughter of good family hears this Sūtra on Cultivating Loving-Kindness, they shall be able to eliminate all karmic obstructions from beginningless time and be freed from all illnesses and calamities. They will be loved and respected by all people. During their lives or at the moment of death, they will certainly behold the Buddhas of the ten directions and receive the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; or they will attain samādhi, or dharma-patience, or enter the gates of dhāraṇī. Their minds will be peaceful and secure, free from the fear of death;
they will forever leave behind the sufferings of all evil realms and will surely be reborn in the pure land of Sukhāvatī.
“O Son of the Buddha!

For example, suppose there were a person who, within the three realms, filled them with the seven treasures and offered them to the Tathāgata three times each day for the duration of an entire kalpa; you should know that the merit of such a person would be likewise.
How much more so for one who is able to practice this cultivation?”
"Even if immeasurable Buddhas, Tathāgatas, were to speak of its merits for the duration of an eon, they would still not be able to exhaust them.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, along with the assembly of Brahmās who had come from the lands of the ten directions, all rejoiced greatly, and they faithfully accepted, upheld, and practiced it.
The Section on Cultivating Loving-Kindness from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s Great Vaipulya Teachings.
